title: Do motivational speakers motivate people?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whether motivational speakers actually motivate people. They weigh sincere, life-story-driven speakers against hucksters and pyramid-scheme-like seminars, trace the field's roots from New Thought (Mary Baker Eddy and Phineas Parkhurst Quimby) through Emerson, Dale Carnegie, Napoleon Hill, and Maslow's hierarchy of needs, and profile Tony Robbins (Breakthrough, the firewalk, the Dallas burn injuries, his conference ticket revenue). They also cover the Get Motivated seminar series and its tie to TD Ameritrade and Invest Tools (including the SEC settlement), Nancy Besser, Steve Salerna's book SHAM, and the lack of skeptic coverage. The hosts note they have done corporate speaking themselves. The episode closes with a listener mail about fishing line littering and ghost fishing.

entities.name: SHAM: How the Self Help Movement Made America Helpless

segments.title: Opening banter and opinions on motivational speaking
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about haircuts, then give their initial opinions: the field is flimsy and prone to hucksterism, though a sincere life story can make a speaker legitimate. They discuss Nancy Besser's website and how it changed Josh's view. They compare sincere speakers to seminar sellers and note the field is like the Wild West.

segments.title: Who Moved My Cheese and fictional motivational speakers
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the book Who Moved My Cheese? and how employers use it during downsizing to encourage acceptance. They mention fictional speakers Matt Foley and Frank T.J. Mackey from Magnolia. They describe Matt Long, who overcame a bus accident to run the New York City Marathon and now speaks, and say that making a living through representation is possible.

segments.title: Hosts' own corporate speaking and what makes a speaker
segments.summary: The hosts reveal they have done corporate speaking but told agents they are not motivational speakers. They say anyone can learn public speaking, and that the key difference in motivational speaking is an inspirational story and the through line of inspiration. Nancy Besser says anyone can do it with a particular skill set.

segments.title: Maslow's hierarchy of needs
segments.summary: The hosts explain Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs from the 1940s, with five levels from physiological needs up to self-actualization. They note criticisms, such as the literal reading implying homeless people cannot form friendships, and that the theory forms a basis for motivational speaking.

segments.title: Origins: New Thought, Emerson, Carnegie, Napoleon Hill
segments.summary: The hosts trace the roots of motivational speaking to Mary Baker Eddy and Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, who founded the New Thought movement that claims positive thinking affects fate. They mention Ralph Waldo Emerson as a possible first American motivational speaker, Dale Carnegie's How to Win Friends and Influence People, and Napoleon Hill's Think and Grow Rich.

segments.title: Tony Robbins, Breakthrough, and the firewalk
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Tony Robbins's Personal Power infomercial, his cameo as a McGuffin in the film Shallow Hal, and his 2010 TV show Breakthrough, which flopped. In the first episode he pushed a quadriplegic man out of a plane. They describe his firewalking events, including Oprah walking the coals, the Dallas event where five of about seven thousand people went to the hospital with burns, and the physics of walking on hot coals.

segments.title: Skeptics, Tony Robbins's conference revenue, and Chicken Soup for the Soul
segments.summary: The hosts say skeptics have given the motivational speaking industry little coverage. One critic walked out of a Tony Robbins conference and found it repetitive. They cite Robbins's conference grossing about $42 million at around $4,000 per ticket. They discuss Jack Canfield's Chicken Soup for the Soul, Wayne Dyer, and the idea that speakers now sell books at events.

segments.title: Get Motivated seminars, Invest Tools, and the SEC settlement
segments.summary: The hosts describe Get Motivated, a low-cost seminar series started in 2002 by Peter Lowe, which was once partnered with TD Ameritrade. Attendees heard speakers like Colin Powell, then a sales pitch for options trading courses through Invest Tools. Invest Tools agreed to pay $3 million in 2009 to settle SEC allegations. The lineup includes Kevin O'Leary, Larry King and Edward Snowden. The hosts also discuss Steve Salerna's book SHAM and the self-deflecting blame used by the industry.

segments.title: Closing thoughts and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts summarize that motivational speaking can be good or bad, and advise listeners to approach it intelligently. They tell listeners to search how stuff works for more on the topic.

segments.title: Listener mail: ghost fishing follow-up
segments.summary: Anthony from Charlotte, North Carolina, writes that recreational fishermen leave monofilament line that harms fish, turtles and birds, and urges anglers to dispose of it properly or use environmentally friendly nylon line.
